[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==See Also== * [[Ichinomiya]] * [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Awa Shrine]] ** [[Susaki Shrine]] * {{ill|Hachiman Sōsha Ryo Shrine|ja|八幡総社両神社}} (other [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] of [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]) ==References== {{reflist}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Ken-sha]] [[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Miwa shrines]] }} {{shinto shrines}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}}

旧県社 |創建 = 不明 |本殿 = [[入母屋造]] |別名 = 府中宮・印鑰大明神 |札所等 = |例祭 = 10月19日 |神事 = }} '''大御和神社'''（おおみわじんじゃ）は、[[徳島県]][[徳島市]][[国府町府中]]に鎮座する[[神社]]である。地元の人から府中宮（こうのみや）の呼び名で親しまれている{{要出典|date=2021年3月}}。 == 歴史 == 創祀年代は不詳である。一説に[[大和国]][[大神神社|三輪神社]]から[[勧請]]されたと伝わる。『[[延喜式神名帳]]』に記載された[[式内社]]である。 往古は印鑰（いんやく）大明神と称し、[[阿波国]][[総社]]であったとも言われ、一般に「府中宮（こうのみや）」と呼ばれる。[[明治]]5年（[[1872年]]）に[[郷社]]に列し、[[昭和]]11年（[[1936年]]）に[[県社]]に昇格した。 ただし、「阿波志」には国司の印鑰云々の由緒は捏造であり、実際は弁財天十五童子の第一「印鑰童子」に由来する。と記されている。 == 祭神 == * [[大己貴神]] == 神紋 == * 鍵の立合 == 末社 == * 境内社に江之島神社、若宮神社、稲荷神社があり、飛び地境内社として4神社を所管する。 File:Oomiwa 20230620 2.jpg|本殿 File:Oomiwa 20230620 3.jpg|拝殿 File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|江之島神社 File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg| {{神道 横}} {{Shinto-stub}} {{DEFAULTSORT:おおみわしんしや}} [[Category:徳島県の旧県社]] [[Category:徳島市の神社]] [[Category:阿波国の式内社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:阿波国|社0]]

The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (Annual Festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined Deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|Main Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto topics}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Tokushima City]] [[Category:Former Prefectural shrines]] [[Category:Shikinai shrines]] [[Category:Awa Province Sōja]] ==See Also== * [[Ichinomiya]] * [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Awa Shrine]] ** [[Susaki Shrine]] * {{ill|Hachiman Sōsha Ryo Shrine|ja|八幡総社両神社}} (other [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] of [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]) ==References== {{reflist}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Ken-sha]] [[en:Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)]][[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Miwa shrines]] }} {{shinto shrines}}{{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}}

Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (Annual Festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox Shinto shrine | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (annual festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (annual festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto topics}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Tokushima City]] [[Category:Former Prefectural shrines]] [[Category:Shikinai shrines]] [[Category:Awa Province Sōja]] ==See Also== * [[Ichinomiya]] * [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Awa Shrine]] ** [[Susaki Shrine]] * {{ill|Hachiman Sōsha Ryo Shrine|ja|八幡総社両神社}} (other [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] of [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]) ==References== {{reflist}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]]{{Sōja shrines}}[[category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Ken-sha]] [[en:Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)]][[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Miwa shrines]] [[Category:original pages]][[Category:original pages]] [[Category:Original pages]][[simple:user:immanuelle/Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)]][[category:original pages]] [[en:Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)]]}} {{shinto shrines}}{{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}}

It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). [[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto topics}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Tokushima City]] [[Category:Former Prefectural shrines]] [[Category:Shikinai shrines]] [[Category:Awa Province Sōja]] ==See Also== * [[Ichinomiya]] * [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Awa Shrine]] ** [[Susaki Shrine]] * {{ill|Hachiman Sōsha Ryo Shrine|ja|八幡総社両神社}} (other [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] of [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa Province]]) ==References== {{reflist}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]]{{Sōja shrines}}[[category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Ken-sha]] [[en:Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)]][[Category:Shikinai Shosha]] [[Category:Miwa shrines]] [[Category:original pages]][[Category:original pages]] [[Category:Original pages]][[simple:user:immanuelle/Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)]][[category:original pages]] [[Category:Pages from wikipedia]] [[en:Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)]]}} {{shinto shrines}}{{Miwa and Yamato Faith}} {{⚠️🚨COPIED from EverybodyWiki ❗❕⚠️😡😤Please respect Licence CC-BY-SA ❗}} {{Source Wikipedia}}

[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima [[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct {{draft}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Ohmiwa Shrine.jpeg | deity = all the deities of its province, [[Ōmononushi]]
[[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima {{draft}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Ohmiwa Shrine.jpeg | deity = all the deities of its province, [[Ōmononushi]]
[[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed {{draft}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Ohmiwa Shrine.jpeg | deity = all the deities of its province, [[Ōmononushi]]
[[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima {{draft}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Ohmiwa Shrine.jpeg | deity = all the deities of its province, [[Ōmononushi]]
[[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima {{draft}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Ohmiwa Shrine.jpeg | deity = all the deities of its province, [[Ōmononushi]]
[[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima [[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Sōja This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima [[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima
