Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima {{draft}} {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | image = Ohmiwa Shrine.jpeg | deity = all the deities of its province, [[Ōmononushi]]
[[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima [[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima [[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima [[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Tokushima City]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Former Prefectural shrines]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Sōja [[Ōnamuchi]]
[[Sukunabikona]]
[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社[[ja:大御和神社]]) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== {{Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | deity = Ōkuninushi no Mikoto | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festivals = October 19 (festival) }} '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Tokushima City]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Former Prefectural shrines]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Sōja It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto shrines}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima [[Ōnamuchi]]

[[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] |Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festival = October 19 (festival) }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima Shrine File:Oomiwa 20230620 6.jpg|Other features == See Also == * {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} {{Shinto-stub}} [[Category:Sōja shrines]][[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokushima Prefecture]] This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct [[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] |Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festival = October 19 (festival) }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima [[Mount Miwa]] | type = [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]] |Infobox religious building|religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]]| name = Ōmiwa Shrine | image = [[File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Torii.jpg|270px|Ōmiwa Shrine]] | location = 644 Kokufuchō Fuchū, Tokushima City, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan | coordinates = {{Coord|34|04|10.8|N|134|28|46.6|E|region:JP-36|display=inline,title}} | type = {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} (Small) / Former Prefectural Shrine | established = Unknown | structure = {{ill|Irimoya-zukuri|ja|入母屋造}} | other_names = Kōnomiya (府中宮), In’yaku Daimyōjin | festival = October 19 (festival) }} {{ill|Omiwa Shrine (Tokushima)|lt=Omiwa Shrine|ja|大御和神社}} (大御和神社) is a [[Sōja (Shinto)|Sōja shrine]]. It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct It enshrines all the [[kami]] of the shrines in [[Awa Province (Tokushima)|Awa]] [[Provinces of Japan|Province]]. [[ja:大御和神社]] It is not to be confused with [[Ōmiwa Shrine]] which it is a [[branch shrine]] of Ichinomiya and Soja are not the same thing but were sometimes combinedhttps://archive.ph/wip/XtZfZ {{nihongo|'''Sōja'''|総社|}} is a type of [[Shinto shrine]] where the ''[[kami]]'' of a region are grouped together into a single sanctuary. This "region" may refer to a ''[[shōen]]'', village or geographic area, but is more generally referred to a whole [[Provinces of Japan|province]]. The term is also occasionally called "'''sōsha'''". The ''sōja'' are usually located near the [[kokufu|provincial capital]] established in the [[Nara period]] under then ''[[ritsuryō]]'' system, and can either be a newly created shrine, or a designation for an existing shrine. The "sōja" can also be the "[[ichinomiya]]" of the province, which themselves are of great ritual importance.{{cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Jean |title=Shinto:At the Fountain-head of Japan |date=2011 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-0-415-59348-9 |page=105}} Whenever a new [[Kokushi (official)|kokushi]] was appointed by the central government to govern a province, it was necessary for him to visit all of the sanctuaries of his province in order to complete the rites necessary for ceremonial inauguration. Grouping the ''kami'' into one location near the capital of the province greatly facilitated this duty,{{cite book |last1=Bocking |first1=Brian |title=A Popular Dictionary of Shinto |date=2016 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1138979079}} The first mention of "sōja" appeared in the [[Heian period]], in the diary of Taira no Tokinori, dated March 9, 1099 in reference to the province of [[Inaba]]. {{cite book |last1=Hardacre |first1=Helen |title=Shinto: A History |date=2016 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0190621711}} The name "Sōja" is also found in place names such as the city of [[Sōja, Okayama| Sōja]] in [[Okayama Prefecture]]. ==ja== '''Ōmiwa Shrine''' (大御和神社, Ōmiwa Jinja) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社}} located in {{ill|Tokushima City|ja|徳島市}}, Tokushima Prefecture, Japan. Locally, it is affectionately called "Kōnomiya" (府中宮). == History == The exact date of the shrine’s founding is unknown. It is said to have been established by {{ill|kanjō|ja|勧請}}, with its deity brought from the {{ill|Ōmiwa Shrine|ja|大神神社}} in Yamato Province (modern-day Nara Prefecture). It is listed as a {{ill|Shikinai-sha|ja|式内社}} in the {{ill|Engishiki|ja|延喜式}}. The shrine was historically known as In’yaku Daimyōjin (印鑰大明神) and is believed to have served as the {{ill|Sōja|ja|総社}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Awa Province (Tokushima)|ja|阿波国}}. Locals commonly refer to it as "Kōnomiya." In 1872 (Meiji 5), it was designated a {{ill|Gōsha|ja|郷社}}, and in 1936 (Shōwa 11), it was elevated to the rank of a Prefectural Shrine (県社). However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed keys. == Sub-Shrines == Within the grounds, there are sub-shrines, including: * **Enoshima Shrine** * **Wakamiya Shrine** * **Inari Shrine** Additionally, the shrine oversees four detached precinct shrines. == Gallery == File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Shaden.jpg|main hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Haiden.jpg|Worship Hall File:Omiwa Shrine, Tokushima, Setsumatsusha Torii 2023.jpg|Enoshima However, the "Guide to Scenic Spots in Awa Province (Revised Edition)" disputes the traditional story, stating that the association with the provincial governor's seal (印鑰) is fabricated and instead ties the name to the first of fifteen child deities of Benzaiten, called "In’yaku Dōji." == Enshrined deity == * **Ōkuninushi no Mikoto** (大己貴神) == Shrine Crest == * The shrine crest features crossed
